comments.author: adelie42
comments.body:
Wow, Lots of fun once I figured out how to get it to play. Total honesty, because that is what you want: I appreciate the concept of the tutorial, but it is aggressive and redundant. You have the training ground for tutorial, and the name is a bit misleading. It is just a tutorial. The progressive style nice in theory, but it isn't as though you have some wildly unique controls that need explaining. Just let the player figure it out, failure is a great teacher and I learned way more once I got it to actually play. I think you could lean into the Training Ground harder by having 1v1 match against a "trainer" where what you need to do requires understanding the controls, but just let the player figure it out. You are close to this with "knock the enemy out of the circle", but a little narrative where the player has to do something meaningful and non-intuitive that takes a sequence of actions like you and sensei rush to the circle and you just need to knock them out and you have pretty much everything covered. That said, if jump can be used strategically to create an advantage, I didn't figure it out. Felt more "just there".

The biggest frustration, or at least was a matter of figuring it out and oddly not in the tutorial, is that your attack is rather far away and the band is narrow in distance. I like the wide sweep, but the way if two players are really close to each other you can't hit them felt really awkward. I think there is some potential in that, such as a short range and a melee with a reach could make the game a little more wild, but the close but not too close that is so far away felt weird.

Put together and trusting your vision, the tutorial is explaining the wrong things.

The biggest frustration that had me almost give up is that you have the optional tutorial, but even after doing it when you hit play you are forced through the tutorial again anyway. I say either force the tutorial (please don't) or keep them separate; starting the game should just start the game.

On game balance, without playing for a real long time to find the edges, there is a massive advantage against the AI to get to the next zone early, and you even tell the player where it is going to be. While the AI fight amongst each other earning no points, player can just chill waiting for the zone to move and rack up lots of points while they stop fighting each other and run to the next zone; you are uncontested. My humble suggestion is that whoever is in the target zone has to split the points. This way fighting over a zone and camping uncontested are not equally valid strategies. It feels like the aimed strategy was earn points by knocking out all the other players in the shortest period of time and points are best earned by shortening the time between knocking the first enemy out and the last enemy out. 

The style, the concept, the different levels, and the way everything cleanly goes together. The premise. Beautiful. I genuinely enjoyed playing. Mixing up offensive and defensive approaches to the combat without overcomplicating it would be rich. Add in some combos for the ability to stun or knock people off the roof.

I don't want to overstate how long I played, but that was really enjoyable and look forward to a next release. I expect you had a lot of fun making this. Its better than most content on Newgrounds. ;)

replies.author: Ok-Key2856
replies.body: Thanks a lot! A lot! For your feedback, will implement it and would start working from today itself

replies.author: adelie42
replies.body:
Thank you! I am scared to release my game and get honest feedback, but your reception give me confidence I could handle it. What has helped me recently (developing a game whose progress keeps getting slowed down by my love of playing it) was a clear, sharp vision. I started with developing a constitution that listed prohibited features or extras, and many times now Claude has taken my suggestions and said, "we already decided we weren't going to do anything like that. See Rule 3" or whatever. Virtually every project I have ever worked on has been destroyed by vision creep and this sub has helped me "knock it off".

All to say I am glad you liked my suggestions, but it is your baby. Don't let my feedback distract you from what you want it to be.

I look forward to an update. If you want to DM me when it is available so I don't miss it, I'll definitely give it another look.

replies.author: Ok-Key2856
replies.body: Thanks a lot for your support. I am glad it gave you some confidence

comments.author: Training-Machine-943
comments.body:
Wow! Amazing graphics and realistic figures/players. I am a absolute newbee. Creating basic word searches and quizzes type of games. Once I figured it was fun. I started on a historical stealth prototype in pure HTML5 Canvas. Note: It is primitive compared to what I see in these forums. Togged between Claude and Gemini for the prototype.  
Question: Incredible work on Highground and the Spawn engine. The fluidity and lighting in the browser are top-tier. I’m building a historical stealth web game (Vijayanagara: Stage 1) *Vijayanagara — Stage 1: The God in Exile:* [*https://theselfdrivingmind.com/Vijayanagara\_Stage\_1.html*](https://theselfdrivingmind.com/Vijayanagara_Stage_1.html) centered on a visibility vs. speed mechanic (an open lamp casts light but alerts patrols; cupped flame enables stealth at half speed). 

I’m currently running it on a 2.5D dimetric Canvas engine, but I want to elevate the lighting and atmosphere to the visual fidelity seen in Highground.

Two quick technical questions:

1. When dealing with stealth vision cones and torchlight falloff in the browser, did you find screen-space shader passes or 2D geometric masks better for maintaining 60fps across mobile devices?

2. For an isometric or top-down perspective, what camera smoothing and momentum damping curves do you recommend to make player movement feel grounded rather than floaty?

Would love any guidance on how you approached that level of polish.
